subject: Astronomy & Space
title: M87*: The First Black Hole Photograph
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on M87*: The First Black Hole Photograph.

hook.text: The first black hole ever photographed sits at the center of galaxy M87—6.5 billion times the Sun's mass.

buildup.text: M87 is 55 million light-years away. Its central black hole drives a plasma jet 5,000 light-years long.

discovery.text: The EHT image in 2019 showed a bright orange ring around a dark shadow—exactly matching Einstein's predictions.

twist.text: The image required petabytes of data from eight observatories. It took two years of processing to assemble.

climax.text: Katie Bouman's algorithm helped reconstruct the image. She became the face of the achievement at age 29.

punchline.text: Fifty-five million light-years away. Captured in a single frame.

quiz.question: How far away is the black hole M87*, the first one ever photographed?

details.summary: In 2019, the Event Horizon Telescope revealed the first image of a black hole — the supermassive black hole in galaxy M87, containing 6.5 billion solar masses. The iconic orange ring shows superheated gas orbiting the black hole, with the dark shadow revealing the event horizon's silhouette.
details.whyItMatters: The M87 image was a landmark moment in astronomy. It provided the first direct visual evidence of an event horizon, confirming theoretical predictions and demonstrating that Earth-sized virtual telescopes could image the most extreme objects.
takeaways: First-ever image of a black hole was revealed in 2019
M87's black hole holds 6.5 billion solar masses
The bright ring surrounds the event horizon's dark shadow

faq.question: Why was M87 imaged before our own galaxy's black hole?
faq.answer: M87's black hole is 1,500 times more massive than Sgr A*, making it appear similarly sized from Earth despite being much farther away. Its larger size means gas orbits in days rather than minutes, producing a more stable image. Sgr A*'s rapid variability made imaging it substantially harder.

faq.question: Why is the ring brighter on one side?
faq.answer: Relativistic beaming — the gas orbiting at near-light speed appears brighter when moving toward us and dimmer when moving away, like the Doppler effect for light. This asymmetric brightness is a direct prediction of general relativity and matches simulations precisely.
